e: Christian inscriptions (3rd–8th century)

The database of the University of Bari, the Epigraphic Database Bari (EDB), collects the inscriptions of the Christians of Rome. The open data set contains 40,760 inscriptions, almost all from the catacombs and cemeteries outside the city walls; a number of inscriptions appear in two or three records (the same stone in an older and a newer volume of the corpus); without these second copies (585) we counted 40,175. Of these 27,387 are dated, 3,423 are in Greek (8.5%) and 520 bilingual. 13% of the inscriptions were not carved but scratched into, or painted on, the plaster closing the tomb; 540 are in verse.

The curve shows what percentage of the inscriptions of each period are in Greek, and how many carry a Christogram or a cross. In the 3rd century 31% of the inscriptions are Greek, in the second half of the 4th century 4.7%. The Christogram hardly occurs before the early 4th century (0.7%); in the second half of that century it stands on 20% of the inscriptions. The cross spreads later: 3.8% in the first half of the 5th century, 25% in the 6th. 69% of the dated inscriptions fall in the 4th century; from the 6th–7th centuries only 30–100 inscriptions per band survive, so the curve is uncertain there.

“Main period” is the middle half of the dates, rounded to 25 years. 5,299 inscriptions have a findspot that cannot be assigned to a road. The inscriptions of the Memoria Apostolorum (on the Via Appia, under today’s San Sebastiano) are all scratched or painted graffiti: pilgrims’ invocations of the apostles Peter and Paul.
The month of burial

Christian epitaphs often give the day of burial (“deposita III Kalendas Septembres”). The full date can be read in 1,591 inscriptions (1,479 Latin, 112 Greek). The day in the Roman calendar was converted: “the third day before the Kalends of September” is 30 August.

29% of the burials fall in August and September; if they were evenly spread this would be 17%. The late-summer peak is a known feature of mortality in Rome, linked to malaria and summer infections.

The ages in the two databases are distributed similarly. In the Christian Latin inscriptions 9.6% of the ages are qualified by “plus minus” (about). Of the Christian ages 3,421 come from Latin and 213 from Greek inscriptions; the numerals written with letters in the Greek inscriptions (κε = 25) were converted.

Formulae and offices were counted in the 31,331 inscriptions with a readable text (28,390 with a Latin and 3,437 with a Greek part), once per inscription, together with their Greek equivalents (πρεσβύτερος, ἐν εἰρήνῃ, κατάθεσις). “In pace” or its Greek equivalent stands on 24% of the inscriptions; the pagan “Dis Manibus” survives on 281 Christian inscriptions. Fragmentary numerals and second copies of repeated inscriptions are not counted here either. The office hits and the Greek ages were read one by one: addresses to the reader (“lector”), personal names such as Martyrius and lengths of marriage were left out.
